assumptions: Node.js environment is available on the local machine
The game logic can be implemented entirely in JavaScript/TypeScript
Canvas/WebGL is sufficient for the required visual effects
Simple commodity market price variation algorithms are acceptable
Pirate AI can be basic and still provide engaging combat
payload.candidate_scope: Minimum useful scope: a playable browser-based game with at least 8 star systems, one station per system, a simple commodity trading market, basic hyperspace travel (fuel consumption, pirate encounters), ship-to-ship combat (player lasers vs AI), ship upgrades (cargo, laser, shields, fuel), and save/load functionality. The frontend must be a single-page canvas/WebGL application with visual effects (parallax starfield, hyperspace jump, laser combat), and the server must expose a /healthz endpoint.

payload.observed_context: Factory-initiated initiative with XS complexity and web-app type. The project requires a local Node.js server that serves the frontend, with Chrome as the target browser. No external CDN dependencies allowed—must be fully offline. The game must start immediately after `npm install && npm start` with no manual build steps. Evidence from the initiative specifies: 8+ named star systems with per-system price variation, fuel-consuming hyperspace jumps with pirate-encounter risk, ship upgrades (cargo capacity, laser, shields, fuel tank), save/load functionality, and unit tests for core game mechanics. Performance target is 60fps on a 2020 laptop.
payload.problem_statement: A desire exists to create an Elite-inspired single-player space trading and combat game playable in a web browser. The game should deliver a complete single-page experience with parallax starfield, hyperspace jumps, station docking, ship management (shields, fuel, cargo, credits), commodity trading with dynamic pricing, and arcade laser combat with visual effects.
payload.rationale: The initiative is well-bounded with clear constraints and a specific technology stack (Node.js server, Chrome frontend, TypeScript, no external dependencies). The scope is appropriate for XS complexity, and the functional requirements are understood (8+ systems, trading, combat, upgrades, save/load). Visual polish expectations are reasonable for a browser-based game. The verification requirements (unit tests, browser smoke test, /healthz) are standard and achievable. No evidence suggests technical infeasibility or missing critical information.
